text:
The Pump on Broad Street

In the last days of August 1854, cholera came to Soho. The district was one of the most crowded in London. Families lived several to a room, cellars were full of human waste, and most households got their water by carrying buckets to the public pumps on the street corners. On the night of 31 August people began to fall ill, and they died fast. Cholera brings sudden, violent diarrhoea and vomiting, and a healthy adult could be dead within a day. In the first three days, 127 people died on or near Broad Street. Within a week most of the residents who could leave had fled, and shops stood shuttered on streets that had been noisy days before.

Most doctors of the day had an explanation ready. They believed cholera spread through "miasma," a poisonous bad air that rose from rotting filth and hung over poor neighbourhoods. It was a reasonable-sounding idea. The disease did strike the dirtiest, smelliest parts of the city hardest, and London in summer stank.

John Snow was not convinced. He was a doctor who lived a short walk from Broad Street and was best known as an expert in anaesthesia. The year before, he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during the birth of her eighth child. For years, though, he had been thinking about cholera. He noticed that it attacked the gut, not the lungs. To him that meant people were swallowing something, not breathing it in. In 1849 he had published a short pamphlet arguing that cholera spread through water contaminated with sewage. Few people took it seriously.

The Soho outbreak gave him a chance to test the idea. Snow went to the General Register Office and got the list of everyone who had died of cholera in the area, with their addresses. Then he walked the streets, knocking on doors and asking the same question each time: where did this person get their water?

A pattern appeared almost at once. The deaths were packed tightly around the public pump on Broad Street, which had a reputation for cool, clean-tasting water. Households nearer to a different pump had far fewer deaths. When Snow found victims who lived closer to another pump, he usually learned that they had preferred the Broad Street water and walked the extra distance for it, or that they were children who drank from it on their way to school.

The exceptions turned out to be as useful as the rule. A workhouse on nearby Poland Street held more than 500 poor residents, crowded together in exactly the conditions that miasma theory said were most dangerous. Only a handful died. The workhouse had its own well. Around seventy men worked at the Lion Brewery on Broad Street itself, a few steps from the pump, and none of them died. The brewery also had its own well, and the workers were given a daily allowance of beer, so they hardly touched the pump water.

The most telling case was miles away. A widow living in Hampstead, well outside the outbreak, died of cholera, and so did her niece, who had come to visit. No one else in Hampstead had the disease. Snow found out that the widow used to live in Soho and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it carried to her by cart every day. Bad air could not explain her death. A bottle of water could.

On 7 September Snow presented his findings to the local parish officials, the Board of Guardians. They were sceptical, but they agreed to act. The next day the handle was taken off the Broad Street pump so that no one could draw water from it. New cases dropped away. Snow was honest about one point: the outbreak was already fading by then, partly because so many people had left and partly because the contamination may have weakened. Removing the handle did not end the epidemic single-handedly. But it was one of the first times a public health decision had been made by counting cases and following the evidence.

The question of how the sewage had got into the pump was answered by an unlikely ally. Henry Whitehead, a young curate at the local church, set out to prove Snow wrong. He knew the parish and its families well, and he started his own house-to-house inquiry. The more he found, the more convinced he became that Snow was right. Whitehead traced the likely first case to a baby girl at 40 Broad Street who had fallen ill just before the outbreak. Her mother had soaked the baby's soiled nappies in water and emptied it into a cesspit in front of the house. When the cesspit was dug up, investigators found its brickwork crumbling, only a few feet from the well that fed the pump.

Later that year Snow drew the map that made him famous. It marks each death with a small black bar, stacked outside each house, and the stacks crowd thickest around the pump. It is still one of the most celebrated images in medicine.

Snow did not live to see his idea accepted. He died in 1858, and many experts went on believing in miasma for years. The bacterium that causes cholera was only widely recognised after Robert Koch identified it in 1883. Even so, the method Snow used in Soho, which was to count the cases, map them, look closely at the exceptions, and follow the water, became the foundation of the modern science of tracking disease, called epidemiology. A replica of the pump, without its handle, now stands on what is today Broadwick Street.
